name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: CrewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Multi-Agent AI Workflows
answer: CrewAI is an open-source Python framework, made by CrewAI Inc. and released under the MIT licence, for orchestrating role-playing autonomous AI agents that collaborate on complex tasks. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above the language models and tools it calls. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its production story rests on Flows, a thin deterministic layer for control and guardrails, rather than on unbounded agent autonomy, so teams expecting agents to run themselves should plan for that architecture.

sections.body: CrewAI is a framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, built and maintained by CrewAI Inc. and published under the MIT licence. Its repository, crewAIInc/crewAI, is written in Python and had its most recent push on 3 October 2026, with roughly 59,300 stars at the time of writing. The official site describes it as an open-source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows, in which developers define autonomous agents with specific roles, goals and backstories that can use tools, process tasks and interact with one another. It is powered by language models and simplifies applications that need coordination between multiple agents. In stack terms it is not a model and not a training library: it is the orchestration layer that sits above whichever LLM you supply, whether that is a hosted API such as Cerebras or a model served through NVIDIA NIM microservices, and it coordinates the agents, tasks and tools that do the work.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs CrewAI handles are multi-step, language-heavy automations: research, analysis, drafting and review carried out by collaborating agents. The site's own tutorial builds a researcher agent that uncovers emerging technologies in a topic, uses a web search tool, and produces a three-paragraph report, with a Task representing a unit of work assigned to an agent and a Crew being the collection of agents and tasks that execute together. Process.sequential runs tasks one after another, and kickoff() starts execution with dynamic inputs replacing placeholders. The framework is strongest where tasks require reasoning over unstructured data, API and tool calls, and several specialist roles handing work to one another. The site positions it against RPA platforms, noting that many enterprises use RPA for deterministic UI workflows and CrewAI for cognitive, language-heavy automations, and it recommends CrewAI when tasks need reasoning, unstructured data and collaborating agents. It also covers production concerns such as tracing, guardrails and an Agent Management Platform, and it has been integrated with NVIDIA NIM microservices so that agents and Flows can be powered by models hosted on NVIDIA infrastructure.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The core concepts are few and are explained on the site in plain terms: an agent is an autonomous entity defined by role, goal and backstory, a task is a unit of work assigned to an agent, a crew is a collection of agents and tasks, and a process defines the execution strategy. A working developer can follow the Cerebras tutorial, install the crewai and crewai-tools packages, set an API key in a .env file, and reach a running crew without deep mathematics. What the site does not spell out is a formal prerequisite list, so it is fair to say that comfort with Python, with calling LLM APIs, and with managing secrets in environment variables is assumed rather than taught. The harder learning is architectural rather than syntactic: the site's own guidance argues that most implementations fail because they are either too rigid or too loose, and that production systems need to be observable, governable, cost-controlled, auditable and maintainable. That is a systems design skill, not a library skill, and the official material offers guidance articles and a developer portal rather than a structured beginner curriculum.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around CrewAI includes the crewai-tools package for external tools such as web search, integrations with model providers including Cerebras and NVIDIA NIM, and an Agent Management Platform for production oversight. The site lists agent-ready documentation: a developer portal, an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file, which is a deliberate choice to make the documentation consumable by agents as well as people. Community scale is substantial, with the repository at roughly 59,300 stars and the site citing 40,000 GitHub stars at an earlier point, alongside a claim of 1.4 billion agentic automations and use by 60 percent of the Fortune 500. The site also publishes its own survey research, including a 2026 State of Agentic AI report based on 500 C-level executives and senior leaders at organisations with over 100 million dollars in revenue and more than 5,000 employees, and a report drawing on insights from over 4,500 professionals building AI agents. Those figures come from CrewAI's own material and should be read as vendor-reported rather than independently verified.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: CrewAI is presented as serving both ends of that spectrum, but through two different mechanisms. Prototyping is fast because a crew of role-based agents with tools and sequential tasks can be defined in a short script, as the Cerebras tutorial shows, and the site describes crews and flows shipping from prototype to production. Production control comes from Flows, which the site describes as a deterministic backbone: a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, just flexible decorators, state management and essential primitives, handling conditional branching, state across steps and custom business logic, with the same inputs producing the same execution path, event-driven and modifiable at runtime. The cost of that split is that you must decide where intelligence belongs and where determinism belongs, and the site is explicit that unbounded agency and prompt chains dressed up as agents are the failure modes. There is also a token cost dimension: the site notes that a ten-step agent run with a 30,000-token prompt can reach 500,000 to two million tokens, and that teams often default to expensive frontier models for work a smaller model could do at a fraction of the cost.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site reports production use cases at large enterprises such as PwC and startups such as Parloa, and says DocuSign increased email engagement rates while cutting sales research time from hours to minutes using the Flows architecture. Its survey material claims that 100 percent of surveyed enterprises plan to expand agentic AI use, that 81 percent have fully adopted or are actively scaling it, and that 57 percent prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than starting from scratch, a preference strongest in construction, financial services, manufacturing, and retail and eCommerce. The obstacles reported are data readiness and integration at 35 percent and insufficient talent or skills at 33 percent, which is a direct signal for anyone choosing what to learn. On the evidence available, CrewAI is a current and actively developed choice rather than a legacy one, with a recent repository push and ongoing integrations, though the adoption figures are vendor-published and the site does not offer independent verification or a breakdown of how many of those deployments are long-lived.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: CrewAI is Python-first, and the site frames the choice in those terms: choose CrewAI for open, Python-first multi-agent crews, and choose Microsoft Agent Framework when standardising on Azure AI services, since that framework targets .NET and Azure ecosystems. It also places itself alongside enterprise RPA platforms such as Automation Anywhere, with the polyglot pattern being that RPA handles deterministic UI and legacy system automation while CrewAI handles cognitive, language-heavy work, and many enterprises run both. The site's comparison pages list CrewAI, AutoGen, MetaGPT and others as the frameworks buyers typically weigh before selecting a stack. Within a Python application, CrewAI is the orchestration layer that calls out to whichever model provider you configure, whether that is Cerebras, NVIDIA-hosted models or another LLM, and to tools such as search, so it composes with the rest of a Python AI stack rather than replacing it.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about the failure modes: implementations that are too rigid with heavy scaffolding, or too loose with unbounded agency, and it criticises prompt chains passing as agents, graph structures chosen over maintainability, and autonomous agents without architectural constraints. Cost is a stated weakness, with extended reasoning consuming tens of thousands of tokens before a short answer and an estimated 60 to 80 percent of enterprise token spend going to use cases that have not proven business value. What the official material does not settle is how much of the reported adoption is durable production use rather than pilots, how the framework performs against its named alternatives on identical workloads, and what the full prerequisite path is for a beginner, since no structured curriculum is described. The survey figures and automation counts are published by CrewAI itself, and the site does not present independent benchmarks, so those numbers should be treated as claims to verify rather than settled facts.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
